name: Puttu
subtitle: steamed cylinders of rice flour layered with coconut, eaten hot with kadala curry

ingredients.note: added a sprinkle at a time

prepNotes: If your rice flour is not pre-roasted, dry-roast it in a pan on low for 6-8 minutes until it smells toasty and feels warm but takes no colour. Cool completely before wetting it.
The moisture level is everything. The flour is right when a fistful holds its shape when squeezed but crumbles apart cleanly when you poke it.
Rest the wetted flour 10 minutes before steaming so the water distributes evenly.

steps.text: Dissolve the salt in the warm water.
Sprinkle the salted water over the rice flour a tablespoon at a time, rubbing it through with your fingertips after each addition.
steps.tip: Never pour. Poured water makes lumps that steam into hard pellets.

steps.text: Stop when the flour feels like damp sand and holds a shape in your fist. You may not need all the water.
Pass the whole lot through a coarse sieve or break the lumps by rubbing between your palms, then rest 10 minutes.
Bring water to a rolling boil in the base of the puttu maker or steamer.
Load the mould: a tablespoon of grated coconut at the bottom, then loose flour to two-thirds, then coconut, then flour, finishing with coconut. Do not press down.
steps.tip: Packing the flour is the classic mistake. Loose layers steam through; packed ones come out dense.

steps.text: Steam 7-8 minutes from when a steady plume comes out of the top.
Push the puttu out onto a plate with the handle of a wooden spoon and serve immediately with kadala curry or ripe banana.
steps.tip: Puttu hardens as it cools. Steam it in batches and eat each one as it comes.

storage: Eat straight from the steamer. Leftovers harden within an hour; crumble them and re-steam 3 minutes, or fry the crumbs with coconut, jaggery and cardamom the next morning.
